title: Eating Interventions: Eating too much
text:
In this second part of a 4 article series about eating interventions that can help neurodiverse children, we discuss practical ways to help children who eat too much.
Eating too much is by far the most common issue with neurodiverse children, especially as they grow up. Children eat because food calms them down, it provides actual psychological comfort! Most neurodiverse children also do not have well developed interoception that tells them when they are full. Sometimes, food not being available makes them upset and aggressive.



Eating too much


While food calms them down, overeating affects health negatively. It is necessary to address this.

What to do
Food and eating is a lifestyle issue. The entire family has to follow, model and reinforce the behaviour we expect of them. Working together and supporting each other is important.

Make a weekly menu plan together. Include favourite as well as not favourite foods. The menu gives visibility of when favourite food is scheduled and helps prepare oneself for the not so favourite food. Remember to accommodate fancy food items and some junk food so there is no sense of deprivation.
The menu should cover all meals - midmorning snack, evening tea etc. If it is not on the menu, you do not eat it.
Agree on measurements - we will have one samosa each; or one bowl of popcorn. Do not prepare or buy more than that.
On a daily basis, for every meal, everyone gets into the habit of measuring and eating - two rotis, one bowl of biryani etc. This shows them that everyone is following the same rules.
Remember it is okay to say - “you have eaten your share. We can have this again - in the evening/tomorrow/next week” - as per your menu.
Talk together, plan, do it together - modelling is very important.

Take help of your therapists to handle any behaviours around food. Also, start when the children are young, it helps them get into good routines and helps everyone!

title: The importance of routines and schedules
text:
What makes for a good day, leaving us content? Engagement through the day with age-appropriate physical activity, cognitive stimulation as well as social exposure tends to lead to good days. Such an engagement gives a sense of contentment and satisfaction to the individual. That’s when we say, we are ‘at peace’. This applies across age groups, across diverse populations.
In this modern era of countless distractions, with each activity designed to be addictive, a routine becomes important if one wants to achieve even a modicum of contentment.
However, maintaining a daily or weekly routine is a much detested and more criticized idea. Many people explicitly try to not have a routine, and it becomes a routine not to have a routine. In this pursuit of non-routine, their goals and to-do lists become haphazard. Even when they clear a part of the list, they tend to feel overwhelmed with what is left and are not able to appreciate either their effort or achievement.
Routine is often negatively associated with living in a hostel. Why do hostels have routines in the first place? Is it to make everyone’s life difficult? When a group of people live together, routine helps with predictability and to plan our lives in the presence of each other. We are usually okay with following the routines in schools, workplaces, and when on trips. When it comes to family, we take the caregivers for granted and refuse to follow a predictable routine. We don’t think twice before informing them at the last minute that we don’t want breakfast or we go to eat whenever we want and they are supposed to provide hot food. People think this is luxury and comfortable living whereas it is just their life going off track.

title: The importance of routines and schedules
text:
Do routines really help?
Many autistics and their families find it easier to live with routines and structured days. However, routines are not just for autistics, having a routine works for everyone.
A routine helps with making free time visible to us. Really! Think about it!
When we have a routine, we know how much work can be done and where there is space. That should give anyone a sense of relief. It’s no different for an autistic child or adult. A routine reduces the number of uncertain periods. That means less anxiety.
For a child, the most important thing about a routine is that adults become available at specific times. The child gets to know when their favourite activity is, when their favourite food is, when they need to face a challenging activity etc.

title: The importance of routines and schedules
section: Is it all rosy with a routine?
text:
Is it all rosy with a routine?
Absolutely not.
The worst part of the routine is the accountability. This is where much of the hate comes from.
If you are a parent and you have put ‘playing a board game’ on schedule, you need to make yourself available at that time. You cannot say that you have a meeting.
If you are a teenager and you need to be accountable, there is this whole universe of competing priorities pulling you apart.
This leads the way to a deep philosophical discussion about ‘What I want to do versus what I need to do’. Probably, another time.

title: The importance of routines and schedules
text:
So, what to do now?
Have a routine for yourself, your children and with the people around you.
Having a routine might sound difficult in the beginning, but one will be able to see how it actually facilitates everyday life, and how it adds to the overall quality of life.

title: Atypical Communication
text:
What does it mean when we say, ‘Autism is Being different’?
It could mean different ways of feeling the world, different ways of seeing the world and different ways one responds to the world.
In a purely language sense, there cannot be an exclusive way to sense the world. In a mathematical sense, there can be infinite ways to feel, see and respond to the world. I want to share some snippets.

The child is a 3-year-old boy with Autism. He had figured that his mom would pick him when he says, ‘I love you’. He tried that. She was busy with something. So, she said, ’ I love you too’. That’s it. He was very distressed as it wasn’t the expected response. But he seeks out the pattern and says, ‘I love you three’. Bingo! This worked better than the first one. The mom picked him up and showered all her love.
The 3-year-old child loved to have ice cream. So, the mom and son would finish their therapy session, and he would have a Vanilla scoop every day. He looked forward to it. One day, he did really well at therapy. So, the mother bought him a Butterscotch scoop. She loved that flavour and it was more expensive.

All hell broke loose. The child cried for half an hour. The mother was in tears. Her child was refusing to have his most favourite thing. The ice cream melted. She threw it away.
After he calmed down, they went to the shop, and he pointed to the ice cream. The shopkeeper gave Vanilla out of habit. The child was ecstatic. That’s it! Vanilla is The Ice-cream. Nothing else is.


A 7-year-old child was traveling in a bus in Hyderabad. He saw the Buddha in Hussain Sagar and asked his mother, ‘How did they flood the Buddha?’

These kinds of experiences happen everyday, in almost every instance of interaction for an autistic person.
Some of these may sound cute and exotic.
However, it’s incredibly hard for an autistic person to go through the day, to be heard and understood and to understand others.
What can we do?
We can definitely learn more about Autism, listen to people on the spectrum, educate ourselves to understand better and do our best to coexist peacefully.

title: Listening
text:
Listening to children is a very important aspect of communication. Irrespective of whether a child is neurotypical or neurodiverse, communication cannot exist between an adult and a child without active listening.
Listening versus hearing
I would like to create a distinction between these two actions. Hearing is a casual surface level activity, we have the option of filtering out information when we hear something and don’t like it or relate to it or just zone out. On the contrary, listening is listening with your whole being, being present, being mindful, holding a respectful space, attentive to body language and emotions, if possible leading to an action point.
When to listen?
If you are an adult around an autistic child, learning to listen is a skill that will take the communication a long way. Only when they listen, the adult can translate the atypical communication into something they understand, sometimes teach the child communication that works for them in any environment and keeps the conversation going.
What happens when we don’t listen?
Communication cannot exist without a partner. We cease to be a partner, therefore, the child stops trying and may withdraw from the relationship.
What happens when we learn to listen?
Wonders! Wonderful conversations and relationships. Makes children confident communicators and to take control of their regulation.
A 4 year old child does not speak, uses Avaz to communicate. The therapist was reading a book to her. She seemed little distant. This is the conversation on Avaz.

Therapist: Are you okay? Child: No Therapist: How are you feeling? Child: Tired. Therapist: Do you want a break? Child: Yes. They go and take a break, play for sometime and come back. Then, Therapist: How are you feeling now? Child: Happy Therapist: Shall we do the activities? Child: Yes
If the therapist had ignored the nonverbal communication from the child in the form of her being dull and unengaged, continued with the activity, that could have led to lot of unhappiness, distress, resentment towards learning and a sense of helplessness.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too little
text:
In this third part of a 4 article series about eating interventions that can help neurodiverse children, we discuss practical ways to help children who eat too little.
Some neurodiverse children eat very little food. It becomes a medical concern as the child’s immunity becomes low, they fall ill frequently, cannot play or move as they want to or like to, get irritated quickly which results in overall unhappiness and many behavioural issues. An unhappy child finds it difficult to learn or relate positively to learning.
Again, let us remember that eating is a lifestyle issue. While there are specific interventions to help with eating too little, interventions work well when the right environment and attitudes are in place. It is important for the entire family to follow, model and reinforce the behaviour we expect of the children. Working together and supporting each other is important.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too little
section: Setting up the environment and attitude
text:
Setting up the environment and attitude
The family should have a good routine for waking up and getting physical activity in the morning. It is important to drink water to stimulate bowel movement and build a sense of hunger. This is especially important for #pooreaters.
Having access to food throughout the day does not help with building an appetite. Food should be available at fixed time intervals that are part of a schedule. Even if a child ate poorly at breakfast, giving them a large glass of milk as a mid-morning snack may not be a good idea, as it interferes with the next meal.
Relying on children’s hunger and letting them starve if they do not eat also does not help build good eating habits. Again, most neurodiverse children have poor interoception - they may not understand the relationship between eating, feeling full and that satisfaction leading to good quality time. If we let them starve, they may end up getting accustomed to staying hungry.
Reading books about food, learning about different kinds of food and tastes, communicating ‘I like’ and ‘I don’t like’ for foods, cooking and baking, talking about feelings while having these conversations can help in building food positivity in children.
All members of the family eating together as frequently as you can is important. While you eat together, talk about food and how you enjoy good food. Model to children that one can safely try new food, it is okay to try and that sometimes you may end up liking new food too!

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too little
text:
Intervention for quantity

Notice how much food the child is able to eat, at the beginning. This is the baseline for how much the child needs to eat. Measure this in spoonfuls, bites or mouthfuls.
Make a visual schedule for the previously decided measure and the child ticks each box as they finish each measure. We can also use tokens that the child can remove for the countdown. This helps the child track how much they have eaten and how much more is left. Predictability helps manage anxiety.
Once the child gets comfortable eating that portion for a few days, gradually increase the measure over a number of days. Decide the pace of increment carefully so we do not overwhelm the child with suddenly increasing demands.
Clearly inform the child whenever demand is increased.
With some children, preparing them with a social story helps. Writing a menu together and discussions about food also help the child to prepare himself to eat.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too little
text:
Increasing variety

Once the child becomes comfortable with the schedule of eating, introduce one new food every three days, just one spoonful - preparing by writing a schedule and social story.
Slowly, new foods became staple foods.

title: Haircut for Autism
text: Haircut can be very hard for some children on the Autism spectrum. However, it need not be a difficult experience. You can help your child stop hating haircuts!

title: Haircut for Autism
text:
The difficulties
There can be many difficulties the child faces that go beyond simple behavioural or sensory issues. It is important to consider them all so we follow a proper process to help the child.

This is an activity out of the routine. Many times, haircut comes as a surprise
Salon is usually an unfamiliar setting - the seating, the lighting, and especially the smells are all different. This can cause overwhelming sensory reactions
There may be difficulties associated with someone touching the child’s hair
Wearing the bib is another difficult sensory experience
The tools used - scissors, trimmers etc. are usually considered unsafe. These tools are very close to the child, around the face
Usually water is sprayed on the hair, the barber holds the head, touches the face, brushes hair off etc. All of these can be sensory triggers

title: Haircut for Autism
text:
The goals
Let us also remember that the goal is not just to get a haircut done, but do it without overwhelming the child and also develop a positive attitude so that over time the child becomes comfortable. There is no point doing this by force or with the child screaming and shouting.
Naturally, we need to address all of these potential difficulties in designing an intervention to help the child. Specifically, the intervention should ensure that:

The haircut does not come as a surprise but as a routine activity that is part of a schedule
The child gets adequate exposure to the saloon setting gradually so that the sensory experiences are not overwhelming

The goals for this intervention are:

Cognitive goals

Being aware of when haircut happens - this needs an understanding of the calendar and scheduling so the child knows on which day it happens
Being aware of what happens during a haircut



Behavioural goals

Cooperate and follow instructions.
Exhibit safe behaviours such as not moving, wearing a bib, not touch blade or scissors etc.



Emotional goals

Go through the process of haircut calmly.
Ask for help when needed.

While we design the intervention, we also need to understand the following.

Child’s profile for understanding the language as well as mode of communication
Child’s experiences with respect to the haircut
Specific challenges the child has with respect to the haircut - sensory difficulties

title: Haircut for Autism
text:
The Plan
We ensure the following:

The child understands when the haircut is going to happen so it does not come as a surprise - we use calendar and scheduling for this
The child understands what happens during the haircut and what is expected - we use social stories for this
The child gets comfortable with various sensory and other experiences - we use task analysis and gradual desensitisation for this

title: Haircut for Autism
text:
The tools and approach

Calendar
Engaging with Calendar is an everyday activity. It is crucial that the day of the haircut is marked for the child in the calendar and talked about every day.


Social story
Social stories are very popular in helping the child with haircuts. However, a social story also works to help only when the child is prepared well in terms of Calendar, and going through the process step by step. A social story can also be made into a video as well. This can be read to the child multiple times during the day when they are in a neutral mood.
Here is an example social story written for a child named Srikar.



Pretend play
The child can engage in pretend play around the activities involved in haircut. They can be the barber for their toys, parents can play different roles such that the child understands what is expected.



Task analysis
Break down the haircut into discrete independent steps. This is called Task analysis.

Enter the Salon
Sit on the chair
Wear the cloth around the neck
Allow water spray
Choose scissors/trimmer
Allow the cleaning brush on the face, neck and chest area.
Sit through the haircut
Remove the bib
Say bye

title: Haircut for Autism
text:
Implementation

First, add the haircut day in the calendar. Everyday, while marking the calendar, highlight when it is and how many days are left.
Read the social story everyday, or once two days depending on how much time there is left.
Let the child pretend play haircut. This may include him sitting in a chair, wearing a bib, hair sprayed with water, etc. steps being done at home. The child can also do these things to a facorite toy.
Take the child through the steps in the task analysis slowly. For example, one day, just go to the salon and come back. Another day, enter the salon, sit in the chair, revolve and play with it and come back. Slowly, over a period of time, go further and further into the task. For example, one day the child may go, sit in the chair, play with the scissors, see the trimmer in operation and come back. Do not push to finish all the steps in one day or in a short time. Give time to the child to be comfortable in each step and progress further only when they are comfortable.
The child watching a parent get a haircut can also help. Using the trimmer on hands and feet can help show that it does not hurt. One can think of many different ways to provide the child with the necessary exposure and assurance!
Slowly, over a month or so, the child will get ready for the haircut. Have a good day!

title: Fostering a connection
text:
We worked with a child in 2022, when he was a 4-year old. He was diagnosed with Autism and he was not speaking at that time.
The child did not lift his hand to reach out for any toy, arousal levels being low. We decided to engage him through multiple activities - sensory, visual, auditory etc. We started him on Avaz to establish a communication channel. His mother took parent training from Sambhavam and took leave.
The mother and child came back to us in June 2024. The mother was finding his screaming, crying and aggression difficult to manage.

What we saw was a distressed child who wanted to be heard. We saw he needed space and a sense of control.
Generally, he liked to just roam around. We waited till he chose to come sit in the chair, ready to engage.
Next, we created a predictable structure for what we would do when he comes and sits. He had to fix a single piece of a puzzle and then he could take a break. He could take a prompt if he wanted. We would not step in without his initiative.
We experienced slight success. He calmed down. He started to come to the table and did some activities. However, the episodes of distress continued. When distressed, he would throw away work materials and toys.
The usual practice of trying to block the throwing behaviour was not suitable as he did not like us touching him. So we thought of a replacement activity - he could throw paper balls into a tub. We also started a social story aimed at letting him learn how, where and when he could throw things.
Initially, he was very unhappy as he could not throw the work materials like he wanted but slowly he started to engage in the paper ball throwing in a neutral mood.
Meanwhile, therapists interacting with him discovered he started to enjoy songs and conversations. They started having casual conversations with him using Avaz. They also engaged through songs - he would hum a tune and they would sing the song. This made him happy beyond bounds.
We like to think this happiness comes from being heard, understood, respected and reciprocated.
Such are the pleasures of fostering a connection and facilitating learning!

title: Eating Interventions: Attitude towards food
text:
In this first part of a 4 article series about eating interventions that can help neurodiverse children, we deal with cultivating good attitudes towards food.
Battles around food are an unavoidable part of being a parent. Children and parents seem to have completely different opinions about pretty much every aspect of food - what to eat, when to eat and how to eat.
Eating more than what we need, ‘indulging’, seems to be becoming a cultural norm. It does not help that more and more junk food is being engineered to create cravings. “No one can eat just one” is not a cute advertisement tagline any more, it is starting to sound more and more like a warning on an addictive substance!
At the same time, issues like picky eating, eating in a hurry, refusing to chew, not being able to maintain oral hygiene are on the rise. These issues become much more pronounced and difficult to handle with neurodiverse children, whose sensitivities and anxieties are as such difficult to live with.
As parents, our goal should be to help children eat good food in reasonable quantities at a sustained pace. In this article, we present a few thoughts and hands-on techniques to help neurodiverse children acquire and maintain good food habits.

title: Eating Interventions: Attitude towards food
section: Cultivate a good attitude towards food
text:
Cultivate a good attitude towards food
For many parents, food is synonymous with love. We can never hold back our love or their favourite food! Most of our children love food, they are fully attentive and engaged around it, and it is difficult to think how that love is impacting them. However, our love should empower them, make them healthy and independent.
Eating is a part of lifestyle. Also, modelling is very powerful. So, any change we expect in the food habits of the child has to be implemented by the entire family.
The family should have a good routine for waking up and getting physical activity in the morning. It is important to drink water to stimulate bowel movement and build a sense of hunger. This is especially important for pooreaters.
It is important to plan balanced meals. Have a weekly meeting to plan the menu. Make space for favourite foods like samosas, popcorn or chicken burgers. Decide on the quantities. Even if your child is not verbal, make them a part of the meeting and let them respond with yes or no. All this activity builds predictability and reduces anxiety about favourite foods. You can use the menu as an opportunity to build #communication, create a sense of time through the #calendar, build it into their weekly #schedule, help them get into the habit of checking written instructions or schedules instead of asking the same questions again and again…the possibilities are endless! Remember our children love food and it is a great motivator.
Last but not least, eat together as a family as frequently as you can. Show how to eat measured quantities of food. Talk about food and how you enjoy good food. Model to children that one can eat good, healthy food in moderate quantities and still be happy!

title: The Problems with Compliance
text:
Compliance to instruction is considered to be very important in ABA. The children are expected to listen to instruction and follow. If they do not, the adult/parent/facilitator is supposed to follow through. Sounds good, right? What can possibly go wrong with it?

The basic assumptions behind compliance
The child does not know anything. Everything needs to be taught. Learning cannot happen without compliance. Obedience is essential.


The problems
The child gets used to being told everything all the time. The child does not exercise any agency. The child growing up this way finds it difficult to say ‘no’ or to negotiate. The child is not able to or finds it difficult to make decisions.


Bigger problems
The person may develop problem behaviors like aggression or self injury as ‘compliance’ does not give space to escape a situation. Mindless compliance also does not build an ethical compass, reasoning and one’s own value system. Without this, the person is always dependent on a directive to conduct themselves. This causes a lot of frustration.


What is the solution then?
The answer is ‘Co-operation’. ABA also talks about cooperation as a skill. As humans, we all need each other and so do children with autism. ABA also talks about pairing with the child to build mutual trust. Let us remember that ‘Trust’ is a two way street.


When the focus is on cooperation, the usual assumptions are
The child may have his or her own thoughts. The child is unable to communicate, therefore, we do not have access to much of their thinking. The only observable way is behavior and it is limited.
Once we recognise that our ability to observe is limited, we embark on a journey of discovery as a therapist along with the child.


Play
The ‘Pairing’ starts here. We play with the child. We let the child lead the play and take control. We also stay firm when it comes to being safe. This is not about pleasing the child, this is about getting to know the child and how they interact with the environment and people. Play as a teaching-learning tool plays a significant role in establishing trust.


Rule following
The best way to teach rules is through games. There is no prerequisite skill needed to play games. All children love to have fun. The child may not be interested in games, but a game is an equaliser as it makes everyone follow the same rules. The child sees everyone doing what is asked of him or her and that provides powerful modeling. A very simple way to do it is through turn taking. We can do this for any activity. There are many sitting games, moving games, games using music etc.
Many people say that their children are not interested in games. It does not matter. They may not show their interest as you expect. Keep at it, find new games, find things that appeal to the children sensorially, find anything that might catch the child’s interest. It is challenging, but it is totally worth it. In my practice, I see that children do recognise when you put in your effort and thought to understand them and be with them. Things do move.


Cooperation - how does it help?
It relies on collaboration, fostering a two way relationship between the child and the adult. It relies on communication, where listening is mutual. It gives equal space to the child. The child actively engages in decision making, therefore learns to say ‘no’. Feedback is mutual. Emotional regulation is part of the entire exercise. Gives a lot of scope to work on intangible/abstract aspects of a relationship. High self worth and self esteem. Motivated learners.


Challenges
A child who is used to this relies on reasoning, therefore, an adult must think through before they ask them to do anything. The child may say ‘no’ more frequently, may show more resistance initially. It is a time and resource consuming exercise. Requires a lot of patience from the therapists and parents.


What next?
Once we work on cooperation, rely on reasoning and respecting a child’s agency, it gives so much space to work on ‘Responsibility’, ‘What is okay and not okay’, ‘Boundaries’. This clears the ground for children to become independent.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too fast or too slow
text:
In this final part of a 4 article series about eating interventions that can help neurodiverse children, we discuss ways to help children who eat too fast or too slow.
The other common issue with neurodiverse children is that they eat either too fast or too slow. Some finish an entire meal in 5 minutes; some take up to 2 hours to eat a snack.
Typically, in either case, the child does not chew properly and it affects digestion. The quick eaters usually eat quite a lot of food before their hunger and palate are satisfied. This leads to weight gain and associated negative loops. The slow eaters tend to pocket the food in the mouth - this affects their oral hygiene. Also, the food tastes bland after being in the mouth for a long time and they lose interest.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too fast or too slow
text:
Intervention for the quick eaters
The key is to create some delay between one mouthful and the next, encouraging them to eat slowly and chew properly. The child has a smiley chart and a bowl.

Once the child takes one spoonful of food into the mouth, they fix the smileys from the bowl, on the chart. During this time, they keep chewing and the rule is they cannot take another mouthful till all the smileys are fixed.
Once all smileys are fixed, they take another spoonful of food.
This time, they pick the smileys from the chart and put them in the bowl.
Keep doing this till the food is finished.

Once, we came across a child who would touch food and everything around with both hands. Smiley chart would have been unhygienic. We modified the intervention.

A table mat, with spaces drawn for the child’s plate, glass and hands was created. The child was expected to keep the plate and glass on the mat, as well as keep their hands on the spaces indicated on the mat.
A number line with numbers 1 to 10 was also drawn on the top of the mat.
The child takes a spoonful of food, and uses fingers to count from one to ten on the numberline. They chew while doing this.
Once the numbers are counted, they can take the next spoonful.
The mat structure helped the child keep their hands clean while eating, as well as introducing delay between spoonfuls through counting.

In both the above cases, the children were older than ten. All the prompts used to remind them to follow the sequence were either written or pictorial so there was not much verbal input, repeated instructions or anyone losing temper.

title: Eating Interventions: Eating too fast or too slow
text:
Intervention for slow eaters
With slow eaters, the key is to create a limit on the time the child keeps food in the mouth. To do this, we mark the beginning and ending of each mouthful so the child has a cue for when the food should be swallowed. We also need to help the child keep track of how much they should eat and how much they have eaten. For this, we use checkboxes or tokens.

Establish the average quantity the child can comfortably eat. Measure this in bites, spoonfuls or mouthfuls.
Make a visual schedule for the number of measures to be eaten. We provide tick boxes or tokens for each measure. For example, if the child has to eat 15 spoonfuls, we make 15 checkboxes or give 15 tokens.
The child takes food in the mouth. We start counting from 1 to 10, in a calm voice, to encourage the child to continue chewing. We can also draw a number line and progress on it if we want to avoid verbal input. This tells the child that they have to finish the mouthful within this count.
At the end of the count, the child ticks a box or counts down by removing a token.
We can plan a break for every 3 or 5 measures, so the child can pause and does not get overwhelmed. The intervention ends when the food is finished!

title: About
text:
What we are working towards

Learning that matters beyond a session
We ask not only whether a child can achieve a goal during a session, but how that learning will help them in everyday life. We want children to have more ways to express themselves, participate in family and community life, develop independence and explore new interests.

Inclusion built through shared responsibility
For us, inclusion is much more than being in the same space as other children. It means developing a sense of belonging through relationships, participation and connection with the people and environment around the child.
We work towards this through planning, discussion and collaboration with teachers and families. Supporting inclusion also means strengthening adults’ understanding of neurodiversity and their ability to respond thoughtfully. We consider what adults, activities and environments can change, rather than placing the entire responsibility for inclusion on the child or the therapist.


Families as partners
We believe parents should have visibility into how we work and opportunities to understand, question and contribute to the process.
Our regular conversations with families help us understand children’s experiences beyond Sambhavam. Together, we review whether learning is carrying over into everyday situations, identify where further support is needed and reconsider goals when family priorities or the child’s needs change.

title: Celebrating Deepavali with Autistic Children: Creating a Joyful, Inclusive Festival
text:
Deepavali — the festival of lights — brings families together in celebration, lighting up homes and hearts with joy. Whether you are a child or an adult, the essence of Deepavali is that it offers something for everyone, welcoming all backgrounds and traditions.
In many households, festival preparations are grand and collaborative, but having autistic children at home calls for a few additional steps to ensure their comfort and inclusion. For children with heightened sensory sensitivities, the bright lamps, vibrant fireworks, and loud crackers may provoke anxiety or distress. Recognizing and respecting your child’s unique sensory profile is the foundation for a harmonious celebration.

title: Celebrating Deepavali with Autistic Children: Creating a Joyful, Inclusive Festival
text:
Meaningful Preparation and Participation
The flurry of festival work may tempt parents to keep children away from tasks, but involving them helps foster belonging and pride. Autistic children can actively participate in organizing, sorting, and decorating tasks such as:

Arranging diyas or decorations
Sorting festival supplies in baskets
Setting up lamps in sequence
Decorating gift boxes or envelopes

These hands-on activities allow children to contribute meaningfully while receiving appreciation from family members. There may be resistance to these new tasks—so it’s important to schedule them thoughtfully, pace the experience patiently, and mark activities on a visual calendar several days in advance. Social stories can be used to explain what to expect and offer choices around participation.
If your child loves crackers, discuss safety using pictures or videos, and always supervise closely.

title: Celebrating Deepavali with Autistic Children: Creating a Joyful, Inclusive Festival
text:
Sensory Accommodations for Comfort
For children sensitive to lights, sounds, or busy environments, practical accommodations make a difference:

Use softer, steady lighting if flickering lamps or serial lights cause distress.
Avoid firecrackers indoors or in small spaces; limit them to quieter outdoor settings.
Provide noise-cancelling headphones or ear defenders during fireworks or crowded gatherings.
Choose peaceful times and neighborhoods for daily outings.
Set up a tranquil, dimly lit room with familiar comfort objects as a retreat for sensory regulation.


If accommodations are insufficient, consider a getaway to a quieter locale, such as a farm. The health and peace of your child are the highest priorities—never push beyond their comfort zone.

title: Celebrating Deepavali with Autistic Children: Creating a Joyful, Inclusive Festival
text:
Navigating Crackers: Emotions and Understanding
Bursting crackers is woven into many childhood memories as a source of excitement and togetherness. As parents, it’s normal to feel disappointment if your autistic child cannot participate in the same way. Avoid projecting these feelings onto the child, and resist making crackers a measure of celebration.
Try gentle desensitization only with support from a therapist, and always pause if your child is uncomfortable. The experience should foster patience, acceptance, and respect for difference. Remember: autistic children are distinct individuals, as Kahlil Gibran wrote, “Your children are not your children… They come through you but not from you.” Their happiness arises from their own experiences—parents can offer opportunities, provide guidance, and step back with love and trust.

title: Celebrating Deepavali with Autistic Children: Creating a Joyful, Inclusive Festival
text:
Reflections
Deepavali celebrates light and hope—values that shine brightest when we honor each child’s needs, embrace differences, and build inclusive traditions. Let this festival be a time for togetherness, appreciation, and gentle guidance, for every member of the family.

title: In Defence of Autism Spectrum Idea
text:
Autism’s diversity is not the problem; systems built on scarcity are. As India still struggles with late diagnosis and minimal support, narrowing who “counts” as autistic risks deepening exclusion.
Uta Frith is a renowned autism researcher who originally helped popularise the idea of autism as a spectrum, to reflect the wide range of ways autistic traits manifest across people. In her recent interview, she now argues that the spectrum has “widened to the point of collapse”, claiming that people currently diagnosed as autistic no longer share a meaningful common factor.
One of her central concerns is that the rise in diagnoses, especially among people without obvious early developmental differences, is straining limited services and preventing those with more visible support needs from receiving adequate help. Framed this way, the problem appears to be “too many” autistic people and “too little” support. But this logic quickly leads to excluding those whose needs are less visible or more intermittent from formal recognition and services. It shifts the burden onto them to find help elsewhere or to “cope” without accommodations, rather than questioning why systems are built on scarcity in the first place.
In the Indian context, this argument sits very differently. We do not, in any meaningful sense, have a robust, state‑funded support infrastructure for autistic people to begin with. The fear that “mild cases” will drain resources away from “severe cases” assumes a level of systemic provision that simply does not exist here. Our reality is closer to chronic under‑diagnosis, late diagnosis, and almost complete reliance on families and private provision.
Frith also questions whether there is really a “common denominator” across all these different presentations. But another possibility is that we, as clinicians and researchers, have historically only recognised autism when it conforms to a narrow, externalised, largely male and childhood‑centred prototype. As more women, marginalised genders, and late‑diagnosed adults describe their experiences, the commonalities may be less in the surface behaviour and more in underlying patterns of sensory processing, social cognition, and effortful compensation. Late‑identified people have often spent years learning to perform neurotypical behaviour under conditions of non‑acceptance. It is unsurprising if the “common denominators” are harder to see when much of the work is happening internally.
Her dismissal of “masking” and “sensory needs” as insufficiently scientific is particularly troubling. Masking is not a fashionable buzzword; it is a widely reported experience of having to hide or suppress autistic ways of moving, communicating, and regulating in order to be seen as acceptable. Research on camouflaging has documented links to exhaustion, anxiety, depression, and suicidality in autistic people, especially women and gender minorities. To insist that this is not “scientific” enough because it relies on self‑report is to ignore the epistemic status of autistic people’s own accounts of their lives. It also sets up an impossible standard where every accommodation request must be justified by “objective” proof acceptable to non‑autistic experts.
When Frith suggests that smooth conversation, responsiveness to irony, or reading between the lines should count as “contra‑indicators” for autism, she reinforces a very narrow, deficit‑based picture of what autistic communication must look like. Many autistic adults describe learning, often painfully, how to manage eye contact, small talk, and humour as survival skills. The conversation may look smooth on the outside but be experienced as scripted, effortful, and draining. Late diagnosis is often precisely about people who “pass” well enough to be considered “perfectly normal” in brief encounters, while still struggling profoundly in other domains of life.
Globally, we can already see autistic adults “hollering” their needs—through writing, advocacy, and social media—while being misunderstood, dismissed, or pathologised for doing so. This pattern is not unique to autism. It resembles what we see whenever a marginalised group—women, Dalit communities, disabled people more broadly—asserts its own knowledge about its experiences and challenges long‑standing expert narratives. The discomfort often shows up as a call to tighten categories, recentre professional authority, or protect resources, rather than as a willingness to re‑examine our concepts.
Frith is right to raise questions about assessment quality, the pressures on clinicians, and the need to look carefully at how diagnostic tools are used. But these are arguments for improving practice, enhancing assessor training, and making space for both observational data and lived experience—not for declaring that the spectrum has “collapsed” or that masking and sensory needs are not scientifically real. For those of us working in contexts like India, where autism is still under‑recognised and poorly supported, the greater danger is not an over‑inclusive spectrum but the continued erasure of autistic people whose needs do not fit older, narrow templates.
A version of this article was originally published in The Hindu on 14 April 2026.

title: Emotional Regulation - Co-regulation
text:
This story comes from Subodha Learning Community where we support families with older children on the spectrum.
Many older children have limited communication skills and those skills do not help them when they are agitated. We come across many situations where the child is upset about something and lack of communication pushes the teenager into a meltdown.
When we are trying to co-regulate, first we validate their emotions. We say ‘I see you are upset about something’. To facilitate communication, we rely on yes/no questions. And then we extend it to a dialogue.
The following conversation happened between a teacher and a teenager.
The teenager, let us say G, is a calm and quiet person. But when he gets agitated, he finds it difficult to manage and starts biting his hand. He screams for a long time to let the emotion pass. But he keeps remembering the incident and feels bad for a very long time. G communicates using Avaz AAC.
Setting: Classroom where there are 5 children and three adults. Context: G puts his hands inside pants. Teacher reminds him to keep hands on the table. G: Starts screaming and crying.
The entire class follows the routine of going to the calming room with an adult as part of ‘Group rules’. They go to the calming area. He takes a pause while crying.
T: Are you ready to get up? G: No T: Are you ready to talk? G: No T: Okay! I will wait.
G takes his hands to bite and two adults block him. He starts screaming and crying again.
T: How are you feeling? G: Angry!
T : Your teacher asked you to take your hands out. Did that make you angry? G : Yes T: Okay ! I hear you and understand that you are angry, but you cannot bite yourself
T : Are you ready to keep good hands? G: No.
T: Then I am going to hold. I don’t want you to hurt your hands. G: Wails loudly.
After about 2 mins,
T: Is it okay to put hands in pants, in public? (Their class learnt ‘Public and Private’ in their EVS class) G: No T: That is why your teacher reminded you of it.
T: How are you feeling now? G: Okay
T: Can I leave your hands? Will you keep good hands? G: Yes
T: Do you want a break? G: Yes
T: What do you want in the break? G: Chips
T: You cannot have chips in the calming room. We need to go to class for that. G: Gets up and walks to the classroom.
By that time, it was lunch time. He finished lunch and ate chips.
This time, he did not remember the incident after that.

title: Facilitating Air Travel
text:
This story comes from Subodha Learning Community where we support families with older children on the spectrum.
Recently, one of our students had to travel by air and the parent was concerned about whether the child will understand the various steps and co-operate during waiting. We took it upon ourselves to facilitate air travel.

What we had

The child can do some activities independently, which the mother has been facilitating at our center.
The child is used to following a visual schedule with a timer. He has been practicing this for six months.
The child has successfully used social stories to regulate himself in the past.



What we did

We wrote a social story about the travel and put in his Avaz.
Had a detailed discussion on how to go about the various steps and waiting at the airport.

Here is the schedule.



What the parent did

His mother made a written schedule detailing the entire trip.
His mother carried the materials required for him to work while waiting.
He had a schedule for sequence of things to do along with a timer.

Guess what happened…the family travelled without any issues!!
Here is a video of the child engaging himself with stitching while in the airplane. Notice the timer!

This makes us so proud. Such a clear example of how preparation, scheduling and social stories work. When we talk about building indepence in children, this is the direction.

title: Helping with Clothing Sensitivity
text:
Clothing sensitivity is a common issue that we come across, as we work with children on the spectrum.
As children grow older, these sensitivities may manifest into challenging behaviors like pulling the pants down in public, not wanting to wear underwear, removing all the clothing and throwing it down the balcony.

The common mistake
These behaviors maybe labelled as attention seeking and sometimes punished or reprimanded. It affects the family adversely by limiting the social contexts they can be part of.


What we did instead
Recently, we came across a 7-year-old exhibiting behaviours that indicated clothing sensitivity. We tried a different, more holistic approach.

Make least harmful assumption
We interpreted it as a multifaceted problem, not an attention seeking behavior. It is a negative perspective the child may have developed due to some experiences.


Consider the emotions
We realised the child is distressed looking at the underwear and the family is unable to make him wear it, and we said we will not force the child. We will work on familiarising him with underwear, give him time to make up his mind and take the step of wearing it.


Pretend play
We made a template of a boy without clothes (Tom) and asked the child to dress him up everyday.
It was an interactive activity. The child chose which colour underwear, shorts or pants, colour of the shirt using Avaz (AAC). Tom was dressed everyday as part of worktime during therapy.


Social Story
Once the child mastered this, we made a social story for the child to wear underwear.
Since he likes to watch videos, our therapist drew the pictures with hand, and read out the script and made it into a video.

He watched this for a week and liked it. This was done along with dressing up Tom.


The final steps
Then we informed him that he can touch his underwear one day and take it upto his feet. We were expecting huge resistance and distress. We decided we will let him take his time, how many ever days he takes for this first step. We resolved not to force him at any cost.
But Voila! He did it!
He took it to his feet, put his feet in and pulled up the underwear. He kept it too!
We were overjoyed. We are so proud of him!

title: How Autistic Children Learn
text:
How do autistic children learn?
Just like other children!
Why do they go to therapies?
The stimulation that is to be provided to a child is not available either in schools or homes because of our lifestyles.
The children seek stimulation, somehow satisfy it one way or the other. For a child who is autistic, seeking attention through verbal or non verbal means becomes challenging. That’s when we experience their distress. The children go to therapies to address this distress which arises because of the void between their needs and ability to communicate their needs to their caretakers.

How do therapists understand children?
The therapists presume competence, meaning assume the child understands. Lack of communication does not mean lack of knowing. This is the basis for any teaching and connecting to a child.
When a child does not respond, a therapist does not challenge the child. Instead, holds their hand and facilitates a response by various methods.
Aggression, negative feedback and punishment is not a part of any therapeutic process. These three are not part of any teaching learning process for any child or person.
Can this approach be taken at home?
Only when this approach is taken, we will be able to provide a nurture and nourishment needed for the child physically,cognitively, socially and emotionally.

title: Building Interest in Reading
text:
Individuals on the Autism spectrum seem to have very strong likes and dislikes. They get totally passionate about what they like and hate what they don’t like completely.
One of the common interventions is desensitisation of aversive things so that it becomes bearable for the person. While this may work, it may end up in traumatising the person. It may cause anxiety and panic during the process.
We worked with a 7-year-old recently, who hated math and reading. He was attending a mainstream school until his parents brought him to us. He could communicate his likes and dislikes very clearly. His ‘No’ was a firm NO.
When we thought about his reading and math, we thought it could be lack of skill, lack of confidence, a bad learning experience or he just didn’t relate to it.
We started with some fun activities for reading, introduced phonic way of reading which wasn’t done before. We chose books which had lots of words based on phonetics. We read to him rather than asking him to read. We started with just one line and once he started looking at the book, slowly progressed from page to page. We did not challenge him or test him.

Somewhere, this made him neutral towards reading within a couple of weeks. Slowly, he started looking forward to the reading activity. As we moved from one book to another, he started asking to be read to him during his break time. He would remember the names of the books and ask. Finally, he started reading to himself. Books became one of his favourites. Not only did he start to read on his own, but he also developed a positive attitude towards reading.
All this, within a span of eight weeks. This was so heartwarming to see.

title: Autism Awareness Run at Himagiri Meadows
text:
Some ideas do more than surprise you - they make you see things differently.
Two young women reached out to invite me to be part of an autism awareness event. I was pleasantly surprised. Most awareness efforts I’ve seen are driven by parents of autistic children. This felt different in two important ways—these were individuals not directly connected to autism, and they wanted us to come and engage, to talk, to build understanding.
They shared their plan: a “Run for Autism.” I was impressed.
There was something deeply ironic and powerful about it. In reality, many people tend to “run away” from autism. It asks for introspection, patience, and a willingness to understand differences. Often, both autistic individuals and their families experience isolation. And here were two young girls doing the opposite—not just running for autism, but bringing together a community of nearly 300 families to stand for a cause.
We started early this morning, leaving Farm Hill at 5 a.m. and reaching Himagiri Meadows by 6:30. What followed were meaningful conversations—with people connected to autism as family members, friends, or simply as curious, open individuals willing to learn.

I also learned more about the spirit behind this initiative. These young women were supported by their incredible fathers, who shared how their daughters spent nearly three weeks planning, encouraging participation, and even going door-to-door. Their pride was evident—and so well deserved.
The event itself was heartening. They raised a significant amount through registrations and donations. We had the opportunity to showcase our children’s work and connect with many people.
We left feeling immensely grateful—for the effort, the intention, and the possibility of a more aware and inclusive community.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
What is consistency?
We often think of consistency as doing something the same way every time: brushing our teeth, bathing, eating, or following a daily routine. There is a sequence, a familiar way of doing things, until we no longer have to think about every step.
But there is much more to consistency.
It is also in how we think, how we make decisions, how we respond, and how we behave towards another person. It is in whether we do what we said we would do.
In the context of autism, I want to look at consistency not merely as a way to teach a routine, but as a way to build trust, independence, and, most importantly, agency.

What is consistency?

In the context of autism, I want to look at consistency not merely as a way to teach a routine, but as a way to build trust, independence, and, most importantly, agency.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
When the adult becomes predictable
When we teach or facilitate learning for an autistic child, we often focus on what the child needs to do consistently.
But how consistent are we?
Suppose we are helping a child learn a self-help skill. One day, we give them time to begin. Another day, we immediately give a verbal instruction. Sometimes we demonstrate. Sometimes we take over because we are in a hurry. On another occasion, we expect them to complete the activity without help.
From our perspective, we are responding to the demands of the day.
From the child’s perspective, what can they depend on? When should they begin? How long can they try? When will help arrive? Will the adult wait, prompt, or take over?
The child is not only learning the activity. They are also trying to work out the adult.
A consistent approach is not about giving exactly the same amount of help forever. It is about making the process understandable, including how support will gradually change as the child learns. The aim is for the adult to step back, not to become a permanent part of every step.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
Whose consistency becomes rigidity?
There is a contradiction here that I think we need to examine.
We ask autistic children to practise an activity in a particular way. We want them to remember the sequence and follow it independently. Yet, when an autistic person wants to continue doing something in a familiar way, we may call it a “rigid pattern”.
Meanwhile, adults change an agreed process because we are tired, in a hurry, looking for variety, or simply feel like doing something differently.
We may have reasons for those changes. But do we make those reasons accessible to the child?
There is a difference between helping someone navigate change and expecting them to accommodate unexplained changes all the time.
Before we label a child’s response as rigidity, perhaps we need to ask: What had they understood would happen? What changed? Did we tell them?

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
How consistency connects to agency
Agency is having a say in what happens in one’s own life.
For a child, this may begin with choosing an activity, asking for help, refusing something, or changing their mind.
Yet many decisions are made for autistic children for a long time—sometimes well into adulthood. Parents and facilitators may feel that this is necessary. They may be worried about distress, safety, communication, or whether the person understands the available options.
Those concerns deserve attention. But they should not close the door on participation.
I do not want us to treat agency as a reward that becomes available after a child reaches a particular “functioning level”, speaks fluently, or completes a particular therapy.
The question I want us to ask is: How can this person participate in decisions now, with the communication and support available to them?

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
section: If we offer a choice, do we honour it?
text:
If we offer a choice, do we honour it?
One of the most important places to practise consistency is in our response to a child’s choice.
If we offer two options, are both genuinely available?
Or have we already decided which answer is acceptable?
“Would you like to paint or go outside?” is not a real choice if choosing to go outside leads to persuasion, disappointment, or a lecture about why painting would have been better.
Once we present something as a choice, we need to be prepared to honour it.
This does not mean that every option is safe or possible. Adults have responsibilities. But we can state a boundary honestly rather than disguise an instruction as a choice.
Presuming competence does not mean leaving a child without support. It means making room for their participation rather than deciding in advance that their contribution will not count.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
section: A choice is not a commitment forever
text:
A choice is not a commitment forever
What happens when a child makes a choice and then becomes distressed?
Our response cannot simply be, “You chose it. Now finish it.”
They may need a way to communicate: ● “No.” ● “This is not what I expected.” ● “I need help.” ● “I want to stop.” ● “I have changed my mind.”
The right to choose must include room to reconsider. We can also make our own reasoning visible: “I thought we could go now because it would be quieter,” or, “We cannot do that today because it is closed.”
Over time, we can support children to consider what matters to them: what they enjoy, what feels manageable, what support they need, and what might happen next.
The purpose is not to give them our decision-making framework permanently. It is to offer support while they develop their own.
That requires space to make imperfect decisions without shame, and without being exposed to avoidable harm.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
But parents are human too
Does consistency mean a parent must never be tired, impatient, distracted, or overwhelmed?
No.
A parent needs space. So does the child.
I am not arguing for perfect performance from adults. I am asking us to notice the expectations we create and take responsibility when we change them.
We can choose one thing at a time: one self-help routine, one way of offering choices, or one commitment to respecting “no”.
And when we are inconsistent, we can acknowledge it:
“I said I would wait, but I rushed you.”
“We usually do this differently. Today there is a change.”
“I offered you a choice and then tried to change your answer. That was not fair.” Consistency should include repair, not the pretence that adults never make mistakes.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
section: Will consistency make a child robotic?
text:
Will consistency make a child robotic?
That depends on what we are being consistent about.
If we consistently demand obedience, suppress refusal, and insist on one correct response, we are not building agency.
If we consistently make communication accessible, respect choices, explain changes, and provide dependable support, our purpose is very different.
I am not asking for every movement, response, or day to look identical.
I am asking for a child to be able to trust the process—and the person supporting them.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
What about variety?
Consistency and variety are not opposites.
We can be consistent in our commitments while enjoying different food, clothes, music, places, and activities.
For example, the consistent part of an afternoon might be that the child chooses a leisure activity and can ask to stop. The activity itself can change every day.
The consistency is in the agreement, not in repeating the same experience.
We also need to distinguish variety from unpredictability. A change that an adult enjoys is not automatically an enjoyable change for the child. They need a say in it too.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
text:
What about indulgence?
Don’t we all sometimes want something extra, something different, or something simply because it gives us pleasure?
Of course.
But there is a question worth asking: Do we make room for the child’s enjoyment, or do we permit it only when we happen to feel generous?
Consider a familiar situation around food. There is an agreed meal routine. Sometimes the adult allows something different; at other times, the same request is refused without explanation.
The child may keep asking. Rather than immediately interpreting this as a failure to follow the routine, we can ask whether the arrangement is clear—and whether the child’s hunger, preferences, and requests are being heard.
Food also deserves care beyond an example about consistency. Asking for more is not automatically a behaviour to correct, and a portion plan should not override attention to hunger or individual needs.
My larger point is this: pleasure need not depend entirely on the adult’s mood.
We can talk about enjoyable experiences, make possibilities understandable, and support the child to help plan them. The purpose is not to guarantee that the child will never feel disappointed. It is to make their participation meaningful.

title: Consistency - Key to Agency
section: What are we asking the child to trust?
text:
What are we asking the child to trust?
For me, this is the central question.
Can the child trust that a choice is a choice?
That “no” will be heard?
That help will be available?
That a change will be explained?
That the adult will acknowledge a mistake?
Consistency is not simply getting a child to repeat a sequence correctly. It is also the discipline we bring to our own decisions and behaviour.
The goal is not a child who waits for permission at every step.
It is a person who can increasingly say: “I understand what is happening. I know what support I can ask for. I have a say in what happens next.”

title: Inclusion through modelling
text:

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
text:
In my years of practice, I have observed a recurring pattern in the way we approach early intervention for autism. A child is typically diagnosed around 2-3 years of age. The predominant early intervention model is an hour of therapy everyday or a few times a week. During these sessions, most autism specialists focus almost exclusively on working directly with the child to teach essential skills. While this is a standard starting point, many children quickly hit a plateau in learning and the families are left unsupported and underequipped.
The data, and my own clinical experience, show that child-led progress often stalls after the first year or two. By this time, the child turns about six years and the focus typically shifts toward school enrollment. While school has its benefits, it leaves a massive portion of the child’s day, and their long-term development, unsupported. You see a therapist for an hour a day for a therapy session but you are often left without a consultant to guide you through the other 23 hours of the day. This is the gap where many parents feel lost, and it is exactly where parent coaching steps in.

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: Parent Coaching: A Crucial Category of Support
text:
Parent Coaching: A Crucial Category of Support
If you haven’t heard the term “Parent Coaching” before, it is because it represents a new category of care. In my practice, I define this not as “treating the child,” but as equipping the parent. My goal is to turn you into the primary expert on your child’s growth.
When I coach a parent, I provide three specific layers of support:

Perspective & Technical Skills: I guide you on which skills actually matter for your child’s future and teach you the specific, technical methods to achieve them.
Emotional Support: I serve as your safety net. Raising a child on the spectrum is an emotional marathon, and you need a space to process that weight.
Philosophical Support: I help you frame your child’s development and your role within it, moving from a mindset of “fixing” to a mindset of “building.”

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: The Power of the Natural Environment
text:
The Power of the Natural Environment
One of the most transformative aspects of my coaching model is that it happens where life happens - within your home. Traditional models often “alienate” the child by placing them in a sterile clinic where they perform tasks for a stranger in an artificial setting.
By coaching you in your own home, we preserve the natural environment. This is vital because:

Real-world integration: Your child learns to navigate the home and school environments they actually live in.
Social continuity: We don’t pull the child away from their life; they continue to learn while playing with their sibling, eating with the family, or relaxing in their room.
Preventing Alienation: Instead of the child feeling like a “patient” in a clinic, they thrive within the existing family structure, guided by the people who love them most.

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: A Story of Transformation: From Overwhelmed to Equipped
text:
A Story of Transformation: From Overwhelmed to Equipped
To understand the impact of this partnership, consider a mother I worked with recently. When we began, she was in a state of constant exhaustion. Her 8-yr old child on the spectrum was struggling with basic transitions—moving from playtime to the dinner table would trigger a forty-minute meltdown. Mealtimes had become a battlefield of sensory sensitivities and power struggles, leaving the mother feeling completely unable to de-escalate the situation or help her child regulate. This was despite early intervention, support at school and everything that a typical family does for their child on the spectrum.
We worked together consistently for about eight months. I didn’t work with the child; I worked with the mother. I equipped her with the technical skills to anticipate triggers and the perspective to understand the “why” behind the behavior. Today, the dynamic has shifted entirely. The progress happened within their natural surroundings because the mother became the expert. The “downstream benefit” is that she no longer needs me to intervene in every crisis; she is now equipped to lead her child through whatever challenge comes next.

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: The Lifecycle Perspective: Preparing for Adolescence and Adulthood
text:
The Lifecycle Perspective: Preparing for Adolescence and Adulthood
Parent coaching isn’t just a temporary fix for early childhood; it is a solution for the entire life cycle of autism. I often see parents “outsource” their child’s development to a revolving door of therapists and schools during the early years.
The danger of this approach is that if you delegate the working relationship to others while your child is young, you will lose “access” to them when they hit the difficult teenage years. In India, there are very few specialists or facilities equipped to handle the complexities of autistic adolescents. If you haven’t built that bridge of communication and influence now, you will find yourself with a teenager you cannot reach.
The Seeds of the Solution The solution to the problems of adolescence must be planted in childhood. By building a strong, direct working relationship through coaching today, you are ensuring that you have a path to influence and connect with your child when the stakes are much higher in the future.

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: The Cautionary Tale: Certificates vs. Functional Skills
text:
The Cautionary Tale: Certificates vs. Functional Skills
I am often reminded of my work with an NGO that supported adults aged 25 to 30. I met individuals who had successfully navigated the academic system and earned degrees, but only because their mothers had sat behind them for decades as “scribes,” navigating every bureaucratic hurdle for them.
While these young adults had the paperwork of success, they lacked functional social skills and the practical abilities needed for a single day of independent living. This is the risk of focusing on the wrong milestones. Parent coaching ensures we don’t just “get them through” the system, but that we focus on the functional, real-world skills that lead to true autonomy.

title: Parent Coaching - The Missing Piece in Autism Care
section: Parent Coaching: A Proactive Choice for the Future
text:
Parent Coaching: A Proactive Choice for the Future
Choosing parent coaching is a shift from being a passive observer of your child’s therapy to becoming the empowered leader of their journey. It is about more than solving a behavior problem today; it is about building a sustainable, lifelong relationship. I encourage you to move from the sidelines and become the equipped participant your child needs. The work we do now is the foundation for everything they will become.

Early Intervention

One-to-One Sessions
Our one-to-one sessions build a bridge between what a child can do today and their next steps in learning and everyday life. We plan around each child’s strengths, interests and support needs, with goals across the following areas.

Communication
We support children to bridge the gap between what they want to communicate and how they are able to express it—helping them share their needs, choices, ideas and experiences.


Classroom Learning
We build on what children can already do independently and provide support for the next step in their learning. Our focus is on helping them access classroom activities and develop greater confidence and independence as learners.


Emotional Regulation

Leisure and Play

We support children in developing skills for everyday routines and self-care. These are more than tasks to complete: they are opportunities for children to exercise choice, experience agency and become more independent in daily life.


Motor Skills
We support children to use their bodies to move, play, explore and solve problems, building foundations for increasingly complex skills as they grow.


Reading and Literacy
Our reading programme supports children as they learn to read, become more independent readers and understand what they read. Once a child begins reading, we weave reading into their language goals, connecting literacy with communication and continued academic learning.


Mathematics and Numeracy
Our mathematics programme begins with pre-number skills and building number sense. We help children move from concrete, hands-on learning towards understanding and applying more abstract mathematical concepts. The programme supports mathematical learning through the primary-school years.



Small-Group Sessions
Our small-group sessions support children who find it challenging to join group activities in the classroom or participate in play with peers.
With guidance and opportunities to practise, children work on:

Sharing materials and taking turns.
Joining and playing with others.
Managing the disappointment of losing a game.
Listening to stories and participating in shared activities.
Communicating and enjoying time with peers.

Our focus is on helping children develop the skills and confidence to participate in groups, with support that responds to their needs.


Classroom Inclusion Support
Our classroom inclusion programme supports children to participate, learn and belong within an everyday classroom setting. Running from Nursery to UKG, the programme places a therapist within the classroom to support a small group of three to five children.
We work with the school curriculum, adapting activities, materials and support to make learning accessible to each child. We help children engage with classroom routines, shared materials, instructions and teachers, while continuing to receive the support they need.
The programme supports development across language, thinking and learning, physical skills, social participation, everyday independence and emotional development.
Classroom life is also about relationships and shared experiences. Children have opportunities to build friendships, sing, dance and play together, and participate in celebrations and presentations. Our goal is for children to become active members of their classroom community—not simply to be present in the room.

Training & Support

Parent Support and Collaboration
We work closely with parents to understand each child’s experiences across home, school and therapy. Our monthly parent meetings provide time to share classroom observations, review progress and hear how children are doing in other settings. Together, we explore whether skills developed during sessions are becoming useful in everyday life and plan ways to support their use across different situations. Parents’ observations, questions and priorities are an important part of this process. They help us develop a fuller understanding of the child and shape the next steps in our work.


Workshops and Trainings
We consider ongoing learning an essential part of a therapist’s work. Our therapists participate in monthly training sessions that explore aspects of psychology, behaviour and learning relevant to the children we support. These sessions help us develop a shared understanding, strengthen everyday practice and revisit our approaches with fresh attention. Drawing on years of working with and learning from autistic children, we also conduct workshops for teachers, parents and special educators. These provide opportunities to share practical learning, explore questions together and strengthen the support available to autistic children in their classrooms, homes and communities.
